facts.statement: ELEC0031 Topic 4 is "Cleaning and Cleanrooms".
Level 1 of contamination reduction is the clean factory.
A cleanroom is an environment with a low level of environmental pollutants.
In a cleanroom, air control is the most important thing.
Cleanrooms are typically used in manufacturing or scientific research.
A cleanroom is specified by the number of particles per volume of air at a specified particle size.

Air path in the fab diagram: make-up air handler (MAH) → mixing plenum → recirculating air handlers (RAH) → HEPA filters → down through the process bays → out through the floor → up the service chase back to the RAH.
The lithography areas of a cleanroom (as in the LCN photos) are lit with yellow light.
Room air is continuously recirculated through HEPA filters to maintain the class.
The HEPA filters are in the ceiling, and the fans that recirculate the air are above the filters.
All mechanical support should be in the plant room, outside the clean area.
Cleanroom clothing is required to maintain the classification.
Books and gloves can be sources of contamination.
Electronic-grade chemicals and gases and DI water are used in the cleanroom.
HEPA stands for high-efficiency particulate air.
Class X: each cubic foot of air holds fewer than X particles larger than 0.5 µm.
The class chart (log–log): the allowed count falls steeply with particle size; each line (classes 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10 000, 100 000) passes through its class number at 0.5 µm.
Small particles stay in the air a long time and coagulate; large particles precipitate quickly.
Particles deposit on surfaces by Brownian motion (small particles) and gravitational sedimentation (larger ones).
The factory environment is kept clean by HEPA filters and recirculation for the air, "bunny suits" for workers, filtration of chemicals and gases, and manufacturing protocols.
Pre-entry: wash face and hands, with lots of water.
Pre-entry: rinse the mouth or drink water, especially after eating, and do not smoke before entering.
Pre-entry: avoid muddy shoes.
Pre-entry: put gloves on before suiting up in the bunny suit.
Entry: wear the provided suit, including mask and overshoes, without dragging it on the floor.
Entry: put vinyl gloves over the latex gloves.
Inside: avoid touching your face with gloved hands or tweezers.
Inside: no spitting, coughing or blowing your nose (use the service area); to sneeze, use the service area and face the floor.
Modern IC factories control unwanted impurities with three tiers: 1 clean factories, 2 wafer cleaning, 3 gettering.
Level 2 of contamination reduction is wafer cleaning.
Contaminants may be particles, organic films (photoresist), heavy metals or alkali ions.

In the roadmap table, as the node shrinks from 250 nm (1998) to 18 nm (2018) the critical defect size falls from 125 nm to 45 nm and allowed starting-wafer particles from < 0.35 to < 0.05 cm⁻², while bulk Fe stays at about 10¹⁰ cm⁻³.
The figure places particles on the surface, Fe and Au on the SiO₂, Na and Cu on the photoresist, and N, P dopants in the silicon beside the interconnect metal.
Front-end cleaning: resist strip (H₂SO₄ + H₂O₂, or oxygen plasma) if necessary, then the RCA clean before the next process step; a good clean matters before high-temperature steps.
Back-end cleaning: resist strip by oxygen plasma or organic strippers, which do not attack metals, then a post-metal clean; it is low temperature and less critical.
SC1 is 5 H₂O : 1 H₂O₂ : 1 NH₄OH; it oxidises organic films, oxidises the Si and complexes metals.
Keeping the NH₄OH content small reduces etching of the Si.
SC2 is 6 H₂O : 1 H₂O₂ : 1 HCl; it removes alkali ions and cations such as Al³⁺, Fe³⁺ and Mg²⁺ that are insoluble in NH₄OH (SC1).
facts.corrects: The slide writes "Mg³⁺": magnesium forms Mg²⁺.

facts.statement: Particles are removed with ultrasonic agitation (20–50 kHz) and now megasonic agitation (around 1 MHz).
facts.corrects: The slide reads "ultrasonic and now megasonic cleaning … (20–50 kHz)": 20–50 kHz is the ultrasonic range; megasonic cleaning runs near 1 MHz (beyond the lecture: Kern, Handbook of Semiconductor Wafer Cleaning Technology).

facts.statement: Piranha, H₂SO₄/H₂O₂ 1:1 to 4:1, at 120–150 °C for 10 min, strips organics, especially photoresist.
HF/H₂O 1:10 to 1:50, at room temperature for 1 min, strips the chemical oxide with all its contaminants and leaves an H-passivated (or F) surface.
A DI water rinse at room temperature follows the HF, SC-1 and SC-2 steps.
SC-1, NH₄OH/H₂O₂/H₂O 1:1:5 to 0.05:1:5, at 80–90 °C for 10 min, strips organics, metals and particles; a small NH₄OH fraction reduces surface roughness.
SC-2, HCl/H₂O₂/H₂O 1:1:6, at 80–90 °C for 10 min, strips the alkali ions and metals not removed by SC-1.
The sequence: piranha → HF dip → DI rinse → SC-1 → DI rinse → SC-2 → DI rinse; a final HF dip can be added to remove the oxide.
The RCA clean is the standard process for removing organics, heavy metals and alkali ions.
Level 3 of contamination reduction is gettering: removing metal ions and alkali ions from the device active regions.
Alkali ions are gettered by dielectric layers on the top side (PSG or barrier Si₃N₄ layers).
Metal ions are gettered by traps on the wafer backside or in the wafer bulk.
Backside gettering is extrinsic gettering; bulk gettering is intrinsic gettering.

The periodic table: alkali ions are group I (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs); deep-level impurities are the transition metals (e.g. Fe, Ni, Cu, Au); group III are shallow acceptors, group IV elemental semiconductors and group V shallow donors.
PSG (phosphosilicate glass) getters the alkali ions Na⁺ and K⁺, and metals.
PSG has negative effects: its dipoles affect electric fields, and it absorbs water, which corrodes Al.
Wafer cross-section: devices in the near-surface region, a 10–20 µm denuded zone (or epi layer), a 500+ µm intrinsic gettering region, and the backside gettering region.
Heavy-metal gettering relies on metals diffusing very rapidly in silicon and segregating to "trap" sites.
The diffusivity graph: interstitial metals (Cu, Au, Fe, Cr, Pt, Ti) diffuse many orders of magnitude faster than the dopants (B, P, As) and Si itself; Cu is the fastest.
Trap sites are created by SiO₂ precipitates (intrinsic gettering) or by backside damage (extrinsic gettering).
Intrinsic gettering uses CZ silicon: SiO₂ precipitates are formed in the wafer bulk by temperature cycling at the start of the process.
The temperature cycle: outdiffusion at high temperature (~1100 °C), nucleation at low temperature (~700 °C), then precipitation (~1000 °C).
Around a growing SiO₂ precipitate interstitial oxygen diffuses in (its concentration dips near the precipitate), interstitials are emitted, vacancies absorbed, and stacking faults can form.
Particles of feature size cause about 75 % of the yield loss in modern VLSI fabs.
Yield models use the measured defect density N(dp) and particle size dp.
Particles of about 0.1–0.3 µm are the most troublesome: larger ones precipitate easily and smaller ones coagulate into larger particles.
In the figure the empirical number of particles falls as N(dp) = k·dp⁻³ over 10 nm–10 µm, while the probability that a particle causes yield loss rises to 1 for larger particles.
In the simplest case yield follows Poisson statistics: Y = exp(−Ac·D0), with Ac the critical area and D0 the defect density.
The Poisson model assumes independent, randomly distributed defects and often underpredicts yields.
Negative binomial statistics remove those assumptions and are more accurate: Y = 1/(1 + Ac·D0/C)^C.
C measures the spatial distribution of defects: the clustering factor.
Yields depend on the defect density D0 and the chip area Ac (excluding the usual low-yield areas at the wafer perimeter).
For D0 = 1 cm⁻² the graph shows Poisson falling fastest (about 10⁻⁴ by 9 cm²), negative binomial with C = 10 in between (10⁻³ at 10 cm²) and C = 2 highest (about 0.03 at 10 cm²).
Clustered defects pile onto a few dies and leave others clean, so negative binomial (less random, clustered) yields are higher than Poisson's, which predicts too-low yields.
With C = 2, yield against chip area for D0 = 0.01, 0.1 and 1 cm⁻²; the ITRS chip sizes for 1997, 2006 and 2012 grow towards ≈16 cm² (≈40 × 40 mm²).
Defect densities must become extremely small to keep the high yields needed for economic IC manufacturing as chips grow.
Monitor defects: overall yield depends on each step in the manufacturing cycle.
Cleaning removes particles, organics (photoresist) and metals from wafer surfaces.
Particles are largely removed by ultrasonic agitation during cleaning.
Organics such as photoresist are removed in an O₂ plasma or in H₂SO₄/H₂O₂ solutions.
The RCA clean removes metals and any remaining organics.
Silicon oxidation in water: Si + 2H₂O ⇌ SiO₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ (5).
Metal oxidation: M ⇌ M^z+ + ze⁻ (6).
In a water solution with a Si wafer and metal atoms and ions, the stronger reaction dominates.
Generally (6) is driven to the left and (5) to the right, so SiO₂ forms and the metal plates out on the wafer.
Good cleaning solutions drive (6) to the right: M^z+ is soluble and desorbs from the wafer surface.
Standard oxidation potentials (V): Mn²⁺/Mn 1.05, SiO₂/Si 0.84, Cr³⁺/Cr 0.71, Ni²⁺/Ni 0.25, Fe³⁺/Fe 0.17, H₂SO₄/H₂SO₃ −0.20, Cu²⁺/Cu −0.34, O₂/H₂O −1.23, Au³⁺/Au −1.42, H₂O₂/H₂O −1.77, O₃/O₂ −2.07.
The strongest oxidants are at the bottom of the table (H₂O₂ and O₃): their reactions go to the left, grabbing electrons and forcing (6) to the right.
Fundamentally the RCA clean works by using H₂O₂ as a strong oxidant.
The O₂/H₂O couple is 2H₂O ⇌ O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.
facts.corrects: The slide's table writes "2H₂O ⇌ O₂ + 4H⁺ + 2e⁻", which does not balance charge: four electrons are released.

facts.statement: Gettering has three steps: 1 making the metal atoms mobile, 2 their migration to trapping sites, 3 trapping.
Step 1 usually kicks the substitutional atom out into an interstitial site, e.g. Au_s + I ⇌ Au_i.
Step 2 happens easily once the metal is interstitial, because most metals diffuse rapidly in that form.
Step 3 happens because heavy metals segregate to damaged regions or N⁺ regions, or pair with effective getters such as P (AuP pairs).
In intrinsic gettering the metal atoms segregate to dislocations around the SiO₂ precipitates.
A three-tiered approach minimises contamination in wafer processing: particle control, wafer cleaning and gettering are the "nuts and bolts" of chip manufacturing.
The economic success of chip makers (their chip yields) depends on careful attention to these issues.

Level 1: clean factories through air filtration and highly purified chemicals and gases. Level 2: wafer cleaning, using basic chemistry to remove unwanted elements. Level 3: gettering metal atoms into regions far from the active devices.
The bottom line is chip yield: bad die are made alongside good die, so higher yield means better profitability.
